news.title: Former Kansas Sen. Nancy Kassebaum remembered as trailblazer
news.text:
Former Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker, who broke multiple barriers for women in the Senate, has died at the age of 94. 

The Kansas Republican died of natural causes in hospice care on Aug. 21, her son Bill Kassebaum confirmed to The New York Times.

Memorials came in from across the political spectrum in Kansas. Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement that “Kansas lost part of its soul” with Kassebaum’s death. 

Kassebaum was the first woman to represent her state in the Senate and the first woman to lead a major committee, taking the gavel of the Labor and Human Resources panel in 1995 during the 104th Congress. 

Kassebaum was a relative political neophyte when she was first elected to the Senate in 1978. Her only prior political experience had been serving on the school board of Maize, Kan. — pop. 785, at the time — and as an aide for one year to GOP Sen. James B. Pearson. 

But her roots in Kansas politics ran deep: Her father, Alfred M. Landon, was a governor of Kansas and the 1936 Republican presidential nominee, who lost to Franklin D. Roosevelt in a landslide. 

When Pearson retired, Kassebaum — then Nancy Landon Kassebaum — ran to succeed him, buoyed by name recognition and TV ads featuring her father. She comfortably defeated Democratic former Rep. William R. Roy.

Kassebaum was the lone woman in the Senate when she was sworn in later that year after being appointed to serve out the last days of Pearson's term, upon his resignation on Dec. 23, 1978. She remained the only female senator until Florida Republican Paula Hawkins joined the chamber in early 1981.

She brought a noted independent streak to her office, breaking with her party on key issues, including gun control and abortion. After the 1994 Republican Revolution, Kassebaum helped strike welfare overhaul provisions from the GOP’s “Contract With America” agenda that would have denied benefits to unmarried teenage mothers and the children of welfare recipients. 

Kassebaum speaks to reporters in May 1993 as first lady Hillary Clinton and Sens. Harris Wofford of Pennsylvania and Tom Harkin of Iowa look on. (Laura Patterson/CQ Roll Call)

Her own legislative contributions include the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, with Massachusetts Democrat Edward M. Kennedy, which made it harder for health insurers to deny coverage based on pre-existing conditions and prior group coverage. 

She took a more conservative stance on other issues, opposing proposals to raise the minimum wage and require businesses to provide unpaid family and medical leave, saying she felt it was wrong to mandate benefits — to the chagrin of Democrats who mainly knew her through her moderate social stances. "I always feel like the skunk at the picnic on this issue," she said at the time. 

Kassebaum’s knack for mediating disagreements helped her earn a reputation as a bridge-builder, while her mild manner sometimes verged on discomfort with being a public figure. "Someday I'm going to hit someone over the head for calling me diminutive and soft-spoken," she once said. "But I am."

She was a trailblazer in smaller ways, as well. Irked by unwritten rules around what women could wear on the Senate floor in the early 1990s, Kassebaum and Sen. Barbara A. Mikulski, D-Md., staged a protest of sorts, wearing trousers to a weekend session and encouraging female staffers to do the same. Pantsuits soon became the norm. 

In 1996, Kassebaum married Howard H. Baker Jr., the former Senate Republican leader from Tennessee, creating a true Washington power couple. That same year, she announced her retirement from the Senate, saying she had wanted to spend more time on other challenges, “including the challenge of being a grandmother.” The couple lived for a time in Japan, where Baker served as ambassador under President George W. Bush. 

Kassebaum poses with fellow female senators at her retirement party in 1996. From left, Sens. Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas, Barbara A. Mikulski of Maryland, Carol Moseley-Braun of Illinois and Sheila Frahm of Kansas. (CQ Roll Call file photo)

Toward the end of her life, Kassebaum’s ties to the Republican Party under President Donald Trump had begun to fray. She called for Trump’s impeachment after the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, The Washington Post reported, and endorsed several Democrats, including Kelly for governor and Kamala Harris for president. 

Members of the current Kansas delegation in Congress fondly remembered Kassebaum over the weekend, including Republican Rep. Derek Schmidt, who worked for Kassebaum for five years on Capitol Hill. 

“Senator Kassebaum introduced this kid from a small Southeast Kansas town to opportunities for public service I had not known possible,” Schmidt said on social media.

GOP Sen. Jerry Moran said he campaigned for her in multiple Senate races, calling her a “friend and encourager” who “was never afraid to challenge me in our conversations.”

“Senator Kassebaum’s time in public service embodied the institution of the U.S. Senate at its best,” Moran said.

news.title: Black Dems to Talarico: Why Won't You Show Us the Money?
news.text:
Or so analysts keep insisting. On the other hand, the fundamentals on the ground in Texas, especially among black voters, indicate a far different outcome. Former Kamala Harris staffer Ashley Etienne told Meet the Press this weekend that the only way for a Democrat to win a statewide election is for the black vote to "overperform." After visiting Houston, Etienne isn't feeling anything close to that level of enthusiasm for Talarico, in part because Talarico still hasn't shown them the money:

Former Kamala Harris staffer Ashley Etienne says far-Left Democrat James Talarico is underperforming with Black Democrats:"The only way you win [Texas] as a Democrat is if you overperform with black voters...they are concerned that there's mild enthusiasm among black voters." pic.twitter.com/EL4diFLe6b— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) August 23, 2026

“Listen, my home state of Texas, we feel incredibly encouraged for two reasons,” Ashley Etienne, formerly the communications director for Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris, told “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker on Sunday. “But the challenge is: the only way you win the state of Texas as a Democrat is if you overperform with Black voters.”“I just came back from Houston last night, meeting with operatives on the ground and state elected officials. They are concerned that there’s mild enthusiasm among black voters and that this $25 million that Talarico promised he was going to spend over a month ago has yet to start to flow,” she continued.

Wait ... what? Talarico supposedly has as much as $50 million on hand. His campaign promised to spend half of that in the black community almost exactly a month ago. Talarico has stepped up his pandering to black voters in the meantime, most recently in his mind-boggling decision to weigh in on the Karmelo Anthony appeal before evidence emerged of Anthony's criminal record and malevolent streak. Talarico has upped the ante, literally, with these voters, and he hasn't yet shown them the money?

Etienne says no one in Houston has seen evidence of it, and that Talarico's money advantage is about to go Tango Uniform anyway:

“The investments aren’t there yet. And then you couple that with the fact that Elon Musk said he’s going to spend nearly $200 million on these races, and Texas is a huge target for that. And you’ve got a problem with black voters in Texas: you’ve got 34% of black men voting for Donald Trump. So if you’re going to wait until Labor Day to start campaigning with black voters, you’re playing to lose.”

Donald Trump will be in Texas on Thursday for a rally and fundraiser for Paxton, too. His MAGA Inc PAC has over $400 million in cash even without Musk's pledge to kick in half as much directly to Republican campaigns. Musk has a particular interest in defeating Talarico, as the NY Post pointed out last week:

Elon Musk is likely to shell out nine-figure sums to help Republicans fend off Democrats in this year’s midterm elections — particularly in Texas, where GOP Senate hopeful Ken Paxton faces a massive fundraising disadvantage.Officials briefed on the matter told Wired that Musk is expected to spend between $100 million and $200 million to boost Republicans, though the precise amount could change.The Tesla and SpaceX boss is expected to focus his political war chest on voter turnout in competitive races, with the closely watched Texas contest between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico among the potential beneficiaries.

Democrats have tried to make Musk into a bete noire ever since he bought Twitter four years ago. On this point, though, they have a rational fear of his political intervention. Musk does a lot of business in Texas, and while members of the Senate don't have much direct impact on state business environments, Musk understands that a Talarico win in Texas might spark a political shift within the state, especially with weak-kneed Republicans in the state legislature. Musk almost certainly sees this race as a leading indicator for a potential retrenchment that will put his business interests at risk, and he will use his resources to protect against it – not to mention the necessity of blunting any progressive momentum nationwide. 

There is another nugget in this report that didn't get much attention, although I noted it in a Final Word at the time:

Talarico has raised $68.6 million through June 30, more than seven times the roughly $9.2 million hauled in by Paxton’s campaign, according to Federal Election Commission filings.The Democrat also held $21.5 million in cash at the end of June compared with just $1.8 million for Paxton, the filings showed.

That's still a big advantage for Talarico, campaign-on-campaign. However, it shows a massive burn rate that hasn't moved the needle yet even among the Texas Democrats' base, let alone the center of the state's electorate. It also suggests that the reason Talarico has not yet shown black voters the money is that he doesn't actually have $25 million to burn in relitigating the primaries against Jasmine Crockett. If that's the case, then Talarico will learn a lesson about expectation-setting and delivery in November.

Speaking of Crockett, she also insists that black voters won't turn out for Talarico. Crockett echoes Etienne about the enthusiasm gap, which has enormous implications for any Democrat running statewide in Texas:

💥NEW: Jasmine Crockett says black community isn't "EXCITED" about James Talarico💥"I personally don't feel like the excitement necessarily exists within the black community ... I don't feel like they're excited!"Crockett dominated Talarico in counties with large black… pic.twitter.com/GChJdaNUOd— Jason Cohen 🇺🇸 (@JasonJournoDC) August 21, 2026

Crockett dominated Talarico in counties with large black voting-age populations during the primary, according to a Reuters analysis.Texas also happens to be the state with the largest black population in the U.S. Talarico will need strong black turnout to have any shot at beating Ken Paxton.Comments like this from Crockett won't help.

These comments don't help, but also notably, neither Crockett nor Colin Allred appear inclined to help as well. These are the two most prominent black Democrats in the state, and their firm choices to stay on the sidelines send a clear signal to black voters in this race. Not that it may matter much; Allred did have enthusiastic-to-overperforming support from black voters in 2024 and still lost to Ted Cruz by nine points. There is zero chance that Talarico will get that level of support from black voters, and nearly zero chance of getting replacement levels of support from anywhere else in the Texas electorate. 

The only advantages Talarico has at the moment are cash and highly questionable polling. Expect both of those advantages to dissipate quickly after Labor Day, with or without Musk's contributions.

news.title: In Maine, Vance shouts out Susan Collins at vice presidential visit she skipped
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance used an appearance in Maine to rally support for a Republican senator who has bucked the Trump administration at key moments but remains critical to Republicans’ hopes of hanging onto the Senate majority.

The vice president offered up praise for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is locked in a tight re-election battle, and made sure to tout her “independent” credentials when speaking at a manufacturing facility in Brewer.

“Whenever I’m in Maine, I got to give Susan a little bit of crap, because as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” Vance said. “And as the president of the United States Senate, she sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder. But she makes it harder because she is coming to work every single day and fighting not for a political party or not for any abstraction; she comes to work every single day, and she fights for the great people of Maine.”

Collins, however, was not present at the rally, citing a scheduling conflict.

Collins’ absence and Vance’s emphasis on her voting record — she has frequently voted with the Trump administration but has opposed the president’s agenda at critical times — illustrates the uneasy relationship between the GOP senator and the White House in a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won by nearly 7 points in 2024.

And it demonstrates how they can be mutually beneficial to each other, with Vance appealing to the GOP base and Collins avoiding appearing alongside a prominent member of the Trump administration at a time when the president’s approval rating is underwater. Collins is set to face Democrat Troy Jackson in the November general election. Recent polling shows Jackson with a slight lead.

Over the weekend, Collins took aim at Trump’s trade war with Canada, which borders Maine.

“I really want us to go back to the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship that we have with our Canadian neighbors,” she told reporters, calling new tariffs “a mistake.”

Trump on Saturday escalated his trade war with the close American ally, imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods after talks between the two nations collapsed. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to retaliate “dollar for dollar” after walking away from what he characterized as a bad deal. And on Monday, Trump said the United States would impose 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel from Canada beginning Jan. 1.“Build in the U.S. and there are ZERO TARIFFS. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!” he wrote in a post on X. “On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”

At Monday’s rally, Vance defended the tariffs, calling Canada “a country that has underinvested in its military, that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America.”

Vance initially referred to Canada as a U.S. state, which Trump has repeatedly done, but he insisted his remark was a “Freudian slip.”

“That was actually an accident,” the vice president said.

news.title: Steve Hilton Within Single Digits of Xavier Becerra in California—New Poll
news.text: Republican Steve Hilton has closed his deficit against Democrat Xavier Becerra to eight points in a new poll of California's governor race. Becerra leads Hilton 49.2 percent to 41 percent among 912 registered voters, with 9.8 percent undecided, according to the survey conducted August 14-16. The poll was commissioned by Hilton's campaign and conducted by David Wolfson, a pollster and faculty member in Columbia University's Political Analytics graduate program. It carries a 3.3-point margin of error and used MMS text-to-web methodology. Hilton seized on the numbers. “Xavier Becerra’s support is collapsing as more and more Californians learn about his horrific record as HHS secretary, which sent thousands of Latino kids into the clutches of child sex and labor traffickers,” Hilton told the California Post, which first reported the poll. Federal HHS oversight reports have documented gaps in sponsor screening and follow-up for unaccompanied migrant children, creating potential safety risks, but they do not establish Hilton's claim that HHS sent thousands of children into sex or labor trafficking. Newsweek reached out to the Hilton and Becerra campaigns for comment Monday. Becerra's Lead Holds Elsewhere The result stands out against a summer of consistent double-digit leads for Becerra. A University of California, Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted August 3-9 among 2,310 likely voters in partnership with the Los Angeles Times found Becerra ahead 55 percent to 37 percent, an 18-point margin. “Today's poll is further confirmation that California voters support Secretary Becerra's focus on lowering the cost of living for California's working families and standing up against the hateful and disastrous policies pushed by Trump and his endorsed candidate, Steve Hilton,” Becerra's spokesperson Jonathan Underland responded to the Berkeley poll in a statement to Newsweek. A Public Policy Institute of California survey conducted June 29-July 6 put Becerra's lead at 25 points, 61 percent to 36 percent. A Kreate Strategies poll in mid-June found a similar 25-point gap. The gap between the Wolfson poll and other independent surveys is also reflected in prediction markets, which have barely moved despite the new poll. Polymarket has put Becerra's odds of winning in November at roughly 93 percent to 96 percent in recent weeks, compared with 3 percent to 4 percent for Hilton. Kalshi shows a similar spread, with Becerra near 96 percent and Hilton near 4 percent. An eight-model prediction aggregator run by OddsShopper put Becerra at 96.4 percent and Hilton at 3 percent. A Difficult Path for Hilton and the GOP Becerra and Hilton emerged from a contentious jungle primary in June and will face off in the November general election. Hilton, a former Fox News host and adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron, received Trump's endorsement in April. He has called the endorsement “a very powerful driver of turnout” heading into the midterm election. Becerra served as secretary of Health and Human Services during the Biden administration and previously served as California's attorney general and a member of Congress. But California remains a steep climb for any Republican. The last Republican to win the governorship was Arnold Schwarzenegger, the actor-turned-politician who won the 2003 recall election and was reelected in 2006. No Republican has won a statewide race in California since. Democrats have a nearly 2-to-1 registration advantage, while independents have favored Becerra by roughly 58 percent to 30 percent in Berkeley's polling. Trump's own performance in California has improved with each presidential election without coming close to winning the state. He won roughly 32 percent of the vote in 2016, 34 percent in 2020 and just over 38 percent in 2024. That trajectory is central to Hilton's argument that the governor's race should be decided on state issues rather than national politics, an argument Democrats have sought to counter by tying him closely to Trump. Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom cannot seek a third term, but Republicans still face an uphill battle in a state that remains one of the most Democratic in the country. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won California by 20 points in the 2024 presidential election, a narrower margin than former President Joe Biden's 29-point victory four years earlier. What Happens Next Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball don’t view the race as competitive, with both classifying it as safe or solid for Democrats. Polls will continue to be closely watched to gauge the mood of the electorate in California ahead of the November midterms. Hilton has challenged Becerra to a series of debates in the coming months, but it’s not clear when they will occur. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Cristina Diciu.
news.summary: Hilton has narrowed his deficit to Democrat Xavier Becerra to eight points, according to a new poll conducted by David Wolfson.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: FL Democrat Senate Candidate Angie Nixon: DeSantis Attacks 'Woke' Because He's Scared of Minorities in Power
news.text:
Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) policies must be put back in place, Democrat Senate candidate and Democratic Socialists of America member Angie Nixon said, asserting that Republicans like Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) have attacked “woke” because they are scared of minorities being in power.

Nixon, who denies being a socialist despite her standing as a DSA member, is an advocate for several key far-left polices, including abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), granting swift amnesty, pushing universal health care, and brining back DEI policies.

“You definitely just have to work to level the playing field, and you gotta get these. You gotta close these corporate tax loopholes. You you have to put the DEI policies back in place,” the Florida House member said during an interview.

“And then you actually have to just make sure that you are passing policies that work to level the playing field. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with DEI with leveling the playing field. Why do we not want people to start at the same point and have access to everything?” she said, promoting “equity” over true equality — a socialist tactic embraced by members of the far left, including failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

“Just because you’re giving me a little bit of access to certain things doesn’t make it whole for like generations of trauma, generations of living in poverty. It’s gonna take me 20 more years or whatever to like get caught up just based on like my family history, right?” she asserted. “And so, you know, I just would have to definitely say we got to stop the rollbacks of these anti-DEI measures and that type of thing.”

She also once said it “totally sucks” that Florida teachers cannot be trained on DEI and accused Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) and Republicans of attacking “woke” in order to undermine minorities who she said are growing into power.

“Ron DeSantis had this attack on woke, this stop woke, because he wants people sleeping. He wants to ban the ability for us to go out and protest the way in which we can wake people up and do… mass protests and mass mobilizations, trying to make it so that people could run folks over in the street if they blocked the street while they were protesting, and it is them attempting to stay in power and control,” she said, claiming they want power and control “because they realize that there’s a new rising majority of like black folks, like Latinos, people of color, women, folks who’ve been marginalized, and they realize that we make up this new majority.”

“And if we come into power, they are fearful… They’re fearful that if this group comes into power, all these marginalized people, that they’re going to do to them what they’ve done to many of us for hundreds of years,” she said. “But history shows that that’s not what happens when marginalized communities come into power.”

Nixon’s position of resurrecting DEI is notable, given that DeSantis and Republicans have been working for years to rid the state of the unfair practices. In 2023, for example. DeSantis and Republicans worked to eliminate DEI initiatives in higher education, which DeSantis said had been used as a “veneer to impose an ideological agenda” in universities. 

Nixon’s claims that Republicans are attacking woke because they are threatened by minorities should come as no surprise. She has a history of outlandish statements and once also said she believes that she cannot work with Republicans across the aisle because “they are literally trying to kill us.”
news.summary:
Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) policies must be put back in place, Democrat Senate candidate and Democratic Socialists of America member Angie Nixon said, asserting that Republicans like Florida Gov. news.title: INGERSOLL: Comedian Embarrasses Himself, Exposes Deep-Seated Truth At Same
news.text:
Below is State of the Day, a morning newsletter by Daily Caller Editor-at-Large Geoff Ingersoll. Sign up here.

Greetings, Dear Reader,

Welcome back to State of the Day, where I strip the euphemism and misdirection off national politics and give it to you straight, no ice, no mixer.

Let’s start off the week in fifth gear, shall we?

THERE ARE NOT ‘TWO SIDES’

The modern left cannot function without the Three E’s: euphemism, equivocation and false equivalence.

During a recent New York Times podcast, rising comedian and a member of the “Tires” cast on Netflix, Stavros Halkias said, “I don’t wanna do the both sides bullshit because it’s just not true. One side is worse than the other, objectively speaking. One side is disappearing people and one side wants children to have healthcare, I don’t think that’s equivalent. A lot of stand-up comics happened to have some of the dumbest opinions on Earth.”

That last part was probably referring to one of his bosses over at Tires, Shane Gillis, along with dozens of other popular comics, including Rogan, Chappelle, even Bill Maher.

Do you think Stav will suffer any consequences for that statement? Assassinated in the street? Fired? Shamed? Probably not.

His statement went viral in part because Kamala Harris’s team clipped it and posted it to their main account. Setting aside that Kamala Harris boosting you as a comic should get you immediately sent to comedy jail, there’s a reason Harris found the statement useful.

In the shortest possible way, Halkias had hit the Three E’s. “Healthcare” doesn’t actually mean healthcare. Stav is an on-the-record big time supporter of transing kids. He even blew a gasket once on X over Daily Caller producing a documentary about detransitioners. “Leave my trans friends alone,” he typed into the void. SEND.

Kids in America all get healthcare. Urgent care, the emergency room, or just on their parents insurance (until they’re way too old to even be called kids. Thanks, Obama!).

The way Stav says “healthcare,” he’s likely referring to the chemical and medical castration of confused minors. That’s what qualifies for “care” on the left nowadays. So refusing to castrate kids, in his worldview, somehow means refusing to give them care.

The term functions doubly as an equivocation. It means different things depending on who or what you’re discussing. If pressed on the trans thing, Stav could just retreat to something more palatable, like universal healthcare. (The ol Motte and Bailey, for those familiar.)

“Disappearing people” functions very much like euphemism, but in reverse. It’s a “dysphemism”, which is when you take something neutral and misleadingly cast it in the worst possible light. There have been eight murders in Fairfax County, Virginia. Eight people disappeared. Only two of the perpetrators are known to have been American (one of whom was formerly a Democrat lieutenant governor of the state who murdered his own wife). Four of them are known illegals who will probably finally be deported and should have been a long time ago. This is, in part, what Stav is referring to when he says “disappearing people.” He could also mean more routine deportations. But have they really been “disappeared”? Not in the Stalineque sense, no. Certainly not in the sense that some of their victims have.

Finally, there’s the false equivalence on steroids. One side is “objectively worse,” he says, meaning Republicans. 

The main issue for modern Democrats is if they simply told you what they meant, all the time, in clear terms, you’d see how insane it is.

Cue DSA spokesperson Megan Romer, who yeah-yeah’d her way through an interview with New Yorker’s David Remnick. Her explicit endorsements included abolishing ICE, police, prisons, borders, the Senate, SCOTUS, and private ownership of the means of production. She extolled the virtues of the Cuban economic regime. She advocated for a Muslim takeover of Israel. And that’s not all, folks; she justified jihadist attacks on western civilization. How cute!

Would you have attended the pro-palestine rally the day after the terrorist attack on Oct. 7? He asked.

“Yeah, yeah,” she said. Literally.

Democratic Party Spokesman At Large Hasan Piker recently celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk at a rally in California. He also celebrated the assassination of a healthcare executive. He frequently calls for violence. There are millions like him. There are regular people I know personally in my social feeds every day celebrating summary acts of violence on conservatives. It’s not particularly fringe. Karen Attiah was fired from her columnist position at The Washington Post for racializing and justifying the death of Kirk in not one but two posts. A day after Piker’s rally, a judge decided the Post was wrong for firing her and forced them to rehire her, with back pay!

Like Stavros, Perennial Fence Sitter and Pet Conservative Jonah Goldberg attempted to both sides the issue just this past weekend on CNN. Scott Jennings was having none of it.

“Abdul El-Sayed was a bad choice in the same way that Ken Paxton was a bad choice for Republicans,” he said. “ … both parties have real whack job problems.”

“Maria, the Democrat attorney general of Michigan can’t even go to your party’s nominating convention because she fears for her safety from Abdul El-Sayed supporters,” Jennings replied. 

That’s no joke. State AG Dana Nessel said recently she plans to avoid the Democrat convention in Michigan because she’s afraid for her life because she’s Jewish.

They can’t even hang out with each other.

Ask yourself this: Has a liberal speaker ever needed a quarter million dollar security detail to speak on a conservative campus?

Stavros is right on one count at least. One side is definitely worse than the other … “objectively speaking.”

Trending SOTD’s

Yeah, you read that right.

A sad state of affairs that everyone got all wrong.

Deception. Lies. Elaborate fabrications. Heavy-handed editing. Sexual misconduct.

news.title: Vulnerable GOP senator breaks with Trump on 2 key issues as Vance makes stop without her
news.text: Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a moderate Republican seeking re-election in a blue-leaning state, is not joining Vice President JD Vance on Monday as he stops in her home state of Maine. Collins, who at times has opposed President Donald Trump's legislative priorities, is a top target for Democrats this year as she runs in a midterm race that's among roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP holds onto its slim Senate majority. Vance's stop in Maine comes as Collins opposes Trump's move this past weekend to impose 50% tariffs on a range of goods from Canada, which shares a long border with Maine. And the senator is also opposed to new U.S. Postal Service rules that, if implemented, could rein in mail-in voting. The vice president on Monday delivers remarks in Brewer, Maine, at Compotech, a defense technology manufacturer. It's the second stop this year by Vance in Maine and the second time that Collins has not teamed up with the vice president. SUSAN COLLINS DROPS BRUTAL REMINDER OF DEMOCRAT CHALLENGER ROCKED BY ACCUSATIONS "I am already scheduled on Monday, so I will not be able to join the vice president," Collins told reporters on Saturday. The Senate was in session when Vance held an event in Bangor, Maine, in May, and Collins stayed in Washington. The senator holds a historic attendance record of casting over 10,000 consecutive roll call votes in the Senate dating back three decades. But Collins, speaking to reporters as she marched in the annual Madison-Anson Days parade, her seventh parade this summer, highlighted that she teamed up last week with Energy Secretary Chris Wright when he stopped in Maine to tour a federally funded battery storage project in Lincoln built on the site of a closed paper mill. "I really appreciated Secretary Wright's presence," Collins said. WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL IN MAINE'S CRUCIAL SENATE RACE SHOWS Collins, who was one of a small group of Republicans who voted to convict Trump in a 2021 Senate trial after the House impeached him following the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, has at times voted against the Trump administration's wishes. "I still think imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake," Collins said on Saturday. Collins also referred to the proposed U.S. Post Office rule to implement a Trump executive order to rein in mail-in voting by refusing to deliver absentee ballots in states that have not turned over their raw voter rolls to the Justice Department or Department of Homeland Security. "Mail-in ballots are very important to the people of Maine," Collins said. "I do no support restrictions that make it more difficult for seniors to cast votes on Election Day via the mail." WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN: CHECK OUT THE FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS ON THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Collins says she supports the House version of the federal SAVE America Act (Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act), which mandates documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote and a photo ID for federal elections. But she joined three other Republicans and all Democrats to vote against advancing a Senate version of the bill, which is a top Trump priority. Collins has also taken issue with the Trump administration over its crackdown on illegal immigration, and its aggressive deportation efforts. The administration received backlash following the fatal shootings by federal enforcement agents of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota who were protesting immigration operations. And the issue flared again this summer, after a fatal ICE shooting in Biddeford, Maine. news.title: Attorneys general conceal records tied to longstanding plans to sue Trump
news.text:
Attorneys general across the United States are using a range of strategies to withhold 2024 emails discussing the longstanding plan to file lawsuits against the second Trump Administration over potential policies that had not yet been implemented.

A “confidential” document obtained by The Center Square shows at least 22 Democratic attorneys general plotted litigation against President Donald Trump as early as April 28, 2024 — three months before Vice President Kamala Harris announced her run for president and approximately seven months before Trump was reelected.

The coordinated effort has a nickname, the “Project for Federal Accountability.” It appears to have borne fruit, with approximately 100 multistate lawsuits filed against the Trump Administration since January 2025.

Most attorneys general have declined to explain why they started planning litigation so far in advance. They have also withheld thousands of emails that would provide additional context.

According to the California Attorney General’s Office, a request from The Center Square for public records was denied because releasing the files “would not be in the public interest.”

“Locating and reviewing all potentially responsive records would impose an undue burden,” wrote Deputy Attorney General Liberty Sacker. “Your request could encompass emails pertaining to 82 lawsuits… We anticipate that any responsive email communications would be exempt from disclosure pursuant to the attorney-client privilege, the attorney work product doctrine, the official information privilege, the deliberative process privilege, the pending litigation exemption, and/or the investigative files exemption.”

According to Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, the files cannot be released “because the requested records are protected by common interest privilege.”

The Maryland Attorney General’s Office cited the same reasoning for withholding records, adding that the release of emails or attachments would be “contrary to the public interest.”

Common interest agreements are one way for attorneys general to try and prevent their litigation strategies from being made public when they coordinate across states. Confidential records obtained by The Center Square show the Maryland Attorney General’s Office and Nevada Attorney General’s Office signed a common interest agreement on May 20 and May 21, 2024, respectively. The California Attorney General’s Office also signed it, but the date was left blank.

But records related to hypothetical lawsuits over hypothetical policies that might (or might not) be implemented by a presidential candidate should not be withheld from the public under a common interest agreement, according to Thomas Moukawsher, a retired judge in Connecticut.

“Parties with the same interests need to be able to speak with their lawyers confidentially,” Moukawsher said. “What is their common interest? We can’t establish what their common interests are… If I was sitting as a judge on the case, I’d say you need to have something a little more specific… I despise Donald Trump, but he’s entitled to the law as much as anyone else is.”

The Center Square has appealed each denial and filed additional requests for records predating the common interest agreement.

What if we pay $61,641?

According to the Colorado Attorney General’s Office, emails related to the Project for Federal Accountability could be released upon payment of a fee.

“The estimated cost to complete this request is approximately $61,641,” wrote Communications Director Lawrence Pacheco. “Please advise how you wish to proceed.”

Transparency advocates across the country have expressed disappointment in Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser for repeatedly trying to keep controversial records behind an insurmountable paywall.

“They get to pick and choose now whether they want to release records just by charging some outlandish fee, and the only way anybody can challenge it is to go to court. Few people are going to hire an attorney to do that,” said David Cuillier, director of the Freedom of Information Project at University of Florida’s Brechner Center for the Advancement of the First Amendment. “We should not be charging people to see what their government is doing. Just like we don’t charge a cover charge to attend a city council meeting, do we? No. That would be ridiculous! We don’t charge people to vote, even though elections are expensive. That would be ridiculous!”

Pacheco’s job responsibilities include responding to the media, but he has repeatedly declined to answer how the Colorado Attorney General’s Office calculates its fees, stating nothing in state law requires him to answer questions.

Colorado law requires fees to be “reasonable,” but the Colorado Attorney General’s Office interpretation of that law is that they are not legally required to explain the reasoning.

In response to a similar request for outside counsel receipts, the Colorado Attorney General’s Office upgraded its fees from $290 to $5,130. The increase occurred after The Center Square agreed to pay and after Weiser won his Democratic primary for governor.

“I’ve never heard of that. Outrageous. It’s crazy,” Cuillier said. “Apparently the word is out in government that you can ignore your local newspaper and TV stations: Screw them.”

The Center Square asked if Weiser reserves the right to, again, raise his price tag by more than 17x upon agreement to pay the $61,641. Pacheco did not respond.

Eliot Richardson, CEO of Run Down The Middle, said he did not want to comment on the specifics of the lawsuits but urged more transparency. His organization is nonpartisan and is dedicated to “fighting against the extremes” of politics.

“Government shouldn’t be done in secret,” Richardson said. “If the government is going to charge a fee for things, including public records, there should be transparency about what drives that fee… You wouldn’t go to a restaurant, get a check that isn’t itemized, with no prices on the menu, and just expect to pay it. You want to know what you’re paying for.”

What about the other states?

Both the New York Attorney General’s Office and Washington State Attorney General’s Office have released some records, although they are highly redacted and largely illegible. The Center Square is appealing the redactions.

According to the Oregon Attorney General’s Office, it has identified more than 1,000 emails discussing the Project for Federal Accountability prior to Trump taking office. So far, the records have not been provided or denied for release.

Attorneys general in Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Washington, D.C., and Wisconsin have either not supplied records or otherwise declined to comment prior to the publication of this story.

[Editor’s note: This story originally was published by The Center Square.]
news.summary: 'I despise Donald Trump, but he's entitled to the law as much as anyone else is'
news.author: Adam Herbets,The Center Square

news.title: Charlie Kirk Post Row: Arbitrator Denies 'Gross Misconduct', Orders Washington Post To Rehire Karen Attiah
news.text: An independent arbitrator has ruled that former Washington Post columnist Karen Attiah was wrongfully dismissed last year over social media posts linked to the death of Charlie Kirk, ordering the news organisation to reinstate her with full back pay and lost benefits.For context, Attiah was sacked last September following online commentary she shared concerning race and gun control in the immediate aftermath of the killing of the late conservative activist Kirk. She stated her sudden dismissal arrived without any prior conversation or formal disciplinary process. This prompted her to publish a termination letter on Substack from Wayne Connell, the head of human resources at the newspaper.In that correspondence, Connell alleged that her online statements actively harmed the integrity of the organisation and potentially endangered the physical safety of staff members. Attiah said she categorically rejected that allegation from the outset. It was wild how quickly newsrooms rushed to purge staff during that period, treating the aftermath of the killing as a harsh referendum on permissible commentary.Union Collective Bargaining Secures Full Back PayThe ruling represents a crucial victory for worker protections across the wider news industry at a time when editorial management teams face intense political pressure regarding free speech and public discourse. The Washington Post News Guild championed her case and released a statement asserting that the judgment firmly 'vindicates' their protracted labour fight against arbitrary management decisions.According to statements released by the union, the collective bargaining agreement negotiated between the guild and the newspaper requires that any employee termination must strictly follow progressive discipline or rise to the level of 'gross misconduct'. The guild noted that the arbitrator concluded that the disputed social media posts did not disparage anyone.Crucially, the judgment rejected the newspaper's decision to hold Attiah personally accountable for hostile threats made against her by bad actors online. The Guild statement noted the arbitrator called that reasoning a 'wholly rejected justification for the termination'. When asked about the outcome of the dispute, a spokesperson for the publication stated only that 'we respect the arbitration process and decline to comment further'.Newsroom Tensions Follow Kamala Harris Endorsement RowAttiah was merely one of several journalists and media figures ousted across the industry for remarks made following the fatal incident. (Whether panicking executives ever pause to consider basic due process during an online backlash remains an open question.) This specific workplace battle unfolded whilst the American publication was already grappling with broader operational challenges and mounting internal tensions.The paper had been navigating intense reader blowback following a controversial decision by owner Jeff Bezos the year prior to kill a planned editorial endorsement for then-presidential nominee Kamala Harris. That executive interference alienated subscribers and coincided with a demoralising string of high-profile exits by top journalists who had grown weary of internal strife and corporate stuff.By requiring the publisher to reinstate the columnist with full compensation for all lost earnings and benefits, the arbitrator's binding decision sets a formidable boundary against reactive dismissals. It demonstrates that enforceable union agreements remain an essential line of defence when media companies attempt to sacrifice their own writers to quiet outside political storms.
news.author: Nica Marie Virtudazo

news.title: Poll: Huge percentage of Democrats want this well-known name for 2028 presidential nominee
news.text:
Democrats continue to favor former Vice President Kamala Harris over 12 other candidates if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary were held today, according to The Center Square Voters’ Voice Poll.

The Center Square has conducted four 2028 presidential primary polls since October, and Harris has retained about 30% of her party’s support each time, though the October poll was her best. In the fall of 2025, 33% of registered Democrat and left-leaning Independent respondents indicated they would choose Harris from a list of eight prominent Democratic politicians. By March, when The Center Square added five more party leaders to the list, her support dipped to 31%. In June and August, she remained the Democratic favorite among 27% and 28% of respondents, respectively. She does appear to fare better among Democrats than left-leaning Independents, at 30% and 20% in August.

The most notable change among the other potential contenders is that support for the second-most-popular candidate, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, fell substantially with the addition of more options in March – from 21% to 16% – and he has plateaued in recent months at 14%. Meanwhile, former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, who initially polled at 7%, climbed to 11% in June and then 12% in the August poll.

While Harris polled best in almost every major demographic group surveyed, she was most popular among the youngest voters and Black voters. Forty-seven percent of registered voters ages 18-29 preferred Harris to other prominent Democrats, and no one came close to her 49% among Black voters. Newsom came in a distant second among Black voters at10%.

Each polled racial demographic besides whites strongly favored Harris. She captured 30% of Hispanic and Latino respondents and 37% of respondents who identified as a race other than white, Black, Hispanic or Latino. She was still the most popular candidate among white voters at 18%, but Buttigieg was right behind at 17%, followed by Newsom at 16%.

Harris also fared slightly better among women than men, and was better among respondents with less formal education. She led among urban, suburban and rural voters, posting her strongest numbers among urban voters, and led across all four regions of the U.S., with her best showing in the South.

While Harris held a commanding lead over Newsom and Buttigieg among female voters, her advantage narrowed among men, where Newsom came within 10 points of her.

Newsom and Buttigieg also gained support among older demographics. Buttigieg was the favorite among senior voters. Buttigieg nabbed 20% support of the 65-and-older bracket; Newsom, 19% and Harris, 13%.

Buttigieg also bested Harris among respondents with post-graduate degrees, with 18% support to Harris’ 15%.

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been included in the poll since March and while she generally came in after Newsom and Buttigieg, she was the second-most-popular choice among the 18-29 demographic with 13% support. She was also the second choice among Hispanic and Latino voters, with 17%. She polled better than Newsom with Independents (10% to his 9%) and better than Buttigeig in the Western region of the U.S. (11% to his 9%).

The Voters Voice Poll, conducted Aug. 12-16, surveyed 2,533 registered voters via opt-in online panel and text-to-web cell phone messages. The respondents were comprised of 930 Republicans, 930 Democrats and 673 Independents. Among independent voters, 330 respondents were classified as true independents, which are individuals who do not lean toward either major party when given the choice. The margin of error is +/- 2.0%.

[Editor’s note: This story originally was published by The Center Square.]
news.summary: Leads among urban, suburban and rural voters, posting strongest numbers among urban voters, leading across all 4 regions of U.S.
news.author: Morgan Sweeney,The Center Square

news.title: Washington Post ordered to rehire columnist fired in wake of 'performative mourning for a white man' Bluesky post about Charlie Kirk murder
news.text:
The Washington Post has been ordered to rehire a columnist after firing her for comments she made on social media following Charlie Kirk's assassination.

A private arbitrator ordered the paper to reinstate Karen Attiah and compensate her with back pay on Thursday, The New York Times reported.

Sarah Miller Espinosa ruled that the Post 'did not have good and sufficient cause' to terminate the former opinion editor and 'violated' the terms of her employment, according to a copy of the decision obtained by the paper.

'The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct,' a line read.

The Post originally announced it was firing Attiah the day after the conservative commentator's assassination in September last year, citing a series of posts on her BlueSky account.

One maintained that 'part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for white men who espouse hatred and violence' on September 10. 

In another penned on the same day, Attiah, 40, declared she was 'refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence is….not the same as violence.'

Post HR chief Wayne Connell promptly told the columnist she had marred 'the integrity' of the paper in a September 11 termination letter.

The letter, published by Status on September 15, advised Attiah that she had been fired for violating the publication's social media policies.

'Your public comments on social media regarding the death of Charlie Kirk... harm the integrity of our organization, and potentially endanger the physical safety of our staff,' a portion read.

A spokeswoman for The Post said the paper respected the arbitration process and declined to comment on the matter further when approached by the Daily Mail.

Attiah celebrated the ruling in a statement sent to the Times, saying she hoped the decision 'sends a message to journalists and media institutions everywhere that freedom of expression is always worth fighting for.'

She also added she was 'willing to go back' to work at the Post and was 'relieved to finally have that record set straight.'

'This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination,' she said in her statement, calling the Jeff Bezos-owned publication 'one of the world’s most storied newspapers.'

Private arbitration is an out-of-court method sometimes used to solve legal disagreements

Kirk, whose alleged assassin is being tried and has not entered a plea, was fatally shot during a speaking engagement at Utah Valley University in Orem. He was 31.

The assassination went on to divide the country due to Kirk's views. Journalists like MSNBC's Matthew Dowd were fired for implying it was his 'hateful words' that got him killed, for instance.

At the time, Attiah told Status her posts had referred to 'the state of gun violence in general.'

'It’s a level of cruelty I did not expect,' she said of the Post's decision to part ways with her over them.

Bezos implemented a host of changes to the Post's Opinion Section just months prior, shortly after attending President Donald Trump's inauguration.

A new tone shifted to focus on 'personal liberties and free markets' rather than the content readers had come to know over the years.

The Amazon founder also pulled a last-minute Post endorsement of then-candidate Kamala Harris not long before – a decision met with anger from both staff and readers. A slew of high-profile exits from staffers followed.

Bezos bought the paper for $250 million in 2013 with the intent of making it 'profitable,' he said at the time.

The Post lost more than $100 million in 2025, after several years of heavy financial losses.
news.summary: A private arbitrator ordered the paper to reinstate the opinion editor and compensate her with back pay on Thursday.
news.author: Alex Hammer,Editor

news.title: A 'fed up' Mark Kelly slams Trump and hints at 2028 bid | Exclusive
news.text:
TUCSON — When Sen. Mark Kelly set out for a day of midterm campaigning, it only took about 15 minutes for someone to address the elephant in the room.

“We need to make sure that we've got leaders in the United States Senate, in Congress and potentially in the White House as well,” Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said, coughing toward Kelly. “Who can actually understand what we need to do and support veterans. I’m gonna nudge him a little bit. I have to,” Fontes added as the crowd cheered. 

Kelly, legs crossed, smiled from under his U.S. Navy baseball hat and didn’t say a word. 

Kelly has been on a cross-country sprint aimed at supporting Democrats ahead of the pivotal midterm election in November. 

Fresh off a trip through Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Missouri and Georgia, Kelly spent the day on Aug. 22 in Tucson boosting Arizona candidates on the ballot this fall. He appeared with Fontes, Attorney General Kris Mayes and JoAnna Mendoza, the Tucson Democrat challenging swing district Rep. Juan Ciscomani, R-Arizona. 

But despite Kelly’s focus on the midterms, some like Fontes were looking further ahead. It’s no secret that Kelly is considering a bid for the White House in 2028. 

“I’m thinking about it,” Kelly said in an interview with The Arizona Republic. “It's a decision that requires a lot of reflection and a lot of thought.” 

Kelly compared running for president to being an entirely different sport than running for Senate, which he’s successfully done twice in battleground Arizona. But the future of the country is on his mind, especially when President Donald Trump’s second term ends in 2029.

“I've got two grandkids. I worry about the future for them and for the future for this nation,” Kelly said.

Kelly’s second granddaughter was born that morning. He had taken care of his older granddaughter the night before, went to the hospital and then set off on a day of campaigning. 

“I even picked the right outfit for Sage,” said Kelly, looking at a picture of his two granddaughters in matching beige outfits on his smartphone screen. 

Is Kelly running for president in 2028?

Kelly is among the countless political leaders taking a look at what will be the first wide-open Democratic primary in nearly a decade. They include California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, who vetted Kelly as a possible running mate for her failed presidential bid in 2024. 

Since that summer, Kelly’s national profile has grown. He has $25 million in the bank and has used his platform to raise $1 million for Arizona Democrats. He’s rising in early state primary polls. An August survey from Saint Anselm College found Kelly had 12% of support among New Hampshire primary voters.

He’s also growing his political network beyond Arizona. A group of young political leaders joined Kelly for the day, including Democrats from the newly anointed early presidential primary states of South Carolina and New Mexico. 

“I want to see the astronaut get to the White House,” said Alexander Walker-Griffin, the vice mayor of Hercules, California, part of the young leaders group. 

At his first event of the day, Kelly spoke about his service as a Navy fighter pilot, from flying his first combat mission at 25 years old to his vote for late President George H.W. Bush. 

“I realized that the people we put in charge of this government need to be of a certain caliber,” Kelly told a crowd of roughly 100 people at the La Rosa events venue in Tucson.

Then he pivoted to Trump and the war in Iran. 

“This president got us into this without a strategic goal, without a plan, without a timeline and without a way out. Now he's stuck,” Kelly said. 

Kelly also slammed the Trump administration for deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has spent more than 200 days at sea. Some sailors tried to go overboard as the deployment dragged on, according to news reports.

Trump has said the ship is “beautifully maintained,” and the deployment was “not nearly long enough.” 

“This is a guy who, literally, for much of his life, has been using a gold toilet, and so of course he doesn't understand service to this country,” Kelly said. 

Kelly has had his own battle with Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Trump called for Kelly to be hanged after he filmed a video reminding U.S. service members that they don’t have to follow illegal orders. 

“This isn't about me. This is about 2 million retired service members that they want to shut up. And you know what? It's working on a lot of them because a lot of them have told me, come up to me personally, and said they are changing what they say and what they do because of this president,” Kelly told The Republic. “It's not going to change what I say or do.” 

In the afternoon, Kelly and his wife, former Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, D-Arizona, mingled with veterans and Arizona political leaders at MotoSonora Brewing. 

Giffords’ vintage BMW motorcycle was prominently on display in the Tucson taproom, which was founded by brothers Jeremy and Jeff DeConcini, members of another southern Arizona political family.

Kelly filmed videos for social media with attendees and passed a challenge coin to an influencer. There were so many of Kelly’s own cameras in the room that one attendee asked whether it was a cable news crew.

Sitting at a picnic table outside the brewery afterward, Kelly said flipping the Senate would be a way to hold the president accountable for what he sees as bad decisions and corruption. He referenced the Trump administration’s embrace of prediction markets and online betting. 

“We are a country of laws. We cannot let people break the law. Nobody is above the law,” Kelly said. “I’m not advocating for any kind of, like, a witch hunt. You know, we don't want the public to think that people are unnecessarily going after this person for political reasons. But when laws are broken and people are enriching themselves to the tune of millions, hundreds of millions, or more, it needs to be looked into.” 

That night, Kelly capped the day with a packed evening event at 191 Toole, where his allies wore “#FULL SPEED AHEAD” T-shirts and he demonstrated what a stump speech might sound like. 

Kelly touched on getting money out of politics, frustration about how young people can’t afford to buy houses and, of course, plenty of fire aimed at Trump.

“Are you guys fed up with what's going on in our country right now?” Kelly said. “I'm very fed up.”

Later, Giffords joined him on stage and talked about the aphasia she faces 15 years after she was shot by a gunman at a political event near Tucson. 

“America needs all of us to speak out, even when you have to fight to find the words,” Giffords said. 

Democrats looking for 'backbone'

Democrats have been carefully watching primaries this election cycle to see where the party is headed after the country swung right in 2024. 

Candidates affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America have pulled off surprising wins in some places, such as Michigan, while voters elsewhere have rejected them. 

More broadly, polls show that Democrats believe the country is on the wrong track and say they are looking for candidates that they see as fighters. 

That’s true for Gilbert Mendoza, a Navy veteran who lives in Rio Rico and attended Kelly’s morning event for veterans. He is not related to JoAnna Mendoza but backs her campaign.

Gilbert Mendoza said he attacks Republicans online all the time, and wishes more Democratic leaders would do the same. He's excited by Democrats who have a “backbone” and are willing to go after the GOP. 

He said he would support Kelly if he runs for president and listed a few other Democratic stars that interest him. 

“Honestly, I’d take anybody right now, like any Democrat. I love AOC. I love Ro Khanna,” Gilbert Mendoza said. “There's so many that are starting to step up.”

In Kelly’s view, the direction of the party depends on the person running and the state where they live. The uniting factor is opposition to Trump. 

“The party is going more in the direction of hey, we have to come up with some solutions to solve some of these hard problems that people are facing,” Kelly said. “We’ve got to meet the moment and come up with some real solutions, which is different than the solutions that Donald Trump is offering.”

“I mean, his solution is you give a big tax cut to billionaires and that somehow magically helps everybody else. It somehow trickles down. It doesn't trickle down. That's a bunch of (expletive).”

Stephanie Murray covers national politics and the Trump administration for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. She co-hosts “The Gaggle,” The Republic’s weekly politics podcast. Reach her at stephanie.murray@usatodayco.com, on X and TikTok @stephanie_murr and on Instagram @stephaniemurray.news.

news.title: AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Georgia’s special congressional runoff
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Residents of Georgia’s 13th Congressional District outside of Atlanta will get a new representative to Congress after a special election runoff Tuesday to replace the late Democratic U.S. Rep. David Scott, who died April 22.

The contest between two Democrats will further reduce an already thin Republican majority in the U.S. House.

The finalists for the seat are former Gwinnett County School Board Chair Everton Blair and Marcye Scott, daughter of the late congressman. They were the top two vote-getters among five contenders in the July 28 all-party special election. Scott received about 46% of the vote, compared to about 38% for Blair.

The winner will serve out the remaining few months of David Scott’s final term. Neither candidate is running in for the next full term in this seat, which begins on Jan. 3, 2027.

Blair was the only candidate in the special election who also ran for the full-term seat. He placed third in the May 19 Democratic primary with about 12% of the vote. State Rep. Jasmine Clark won the primary with 56% of the vote and will face Republican Jonathan Chavez in November. Chavez, who ran unopposed for the GOP nomination, challenged David Scott in the 2024 general election and received about 28% of the vote.

Clark did not file to compete in the special election. Doing so would have required her to resign from her seat in the state Legislature just as Republican Gov. Brian Kemp was calling for a special session to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries in time for the 2028 elections. The state constitution bars state officeholders from seeking a different office with a start date more than 30 days before the end of the officeholder’s current term. The special session did convene, but Republican leaders opted not to take up redistricting.

In recent years, Congressman Scott had faced questions over his age and health. At the time of his death at age 80, he was facing a tough primary challenge from Clark and others as he sought a 13th term.

Georgia’s 13th Congressional District is east and southeast of Atlanta and includes parts of six heavily Democratic counties: Clayton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Henry, Newton and Rockdale. Of the six, the district’s portion of Gwinnett County has the lion’s share of voters, with about 46% of the district electorate in the 2024 general election.

Blair’s best performance in the July 28 special election was in his home base of Gwinnett County, where he received 56% of the vote. Marcye Scott, who lives outside the district in Fulton County as her father did, carried the other five counties in the district, scoring her highest totals in DeKalb, Clayton and Henry.

David Scott won his 2024 reelection bid with about 72% of the vote. In the presidential election that night, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 71% of the vote in the district, compared with about 28% for Republican Donald Trump. Trump had his best performance in the district in Gwinnett County, although that still only amounted to about 35% of the vote.

Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:

When do polls close?

Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the special runoff in the 13th Congressional District.

Who gets to vote?

Any voter registered in the 13th Congressional District may participate in the special runoff.

How many voters are there?

As of Friday, there were about 585,000 registered voters in the 13th Congressional District. Georgia voters do not register by party.

How many people actually vote?

A total of 20,510 votes were cast in the July 28 special election. Turnout in a runoff election tends to be lower than in the election that preceded it.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?

About 47% of the total vote in the July 28 special election was cast early in-person or by mail.

As of Friday, about 5,200 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election, with by far the largest share coming from Gwinnett County, followed by Clayton and Rockdale counties.

When are early and absentee votes released?

All six counties in the 13th Congressional District tend to release most or all of their results from early in-person and mail voting in the first vote update of the night, usually before any in-person Election Day results are released.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the July 28 special election, the AP first reported results at 7:05 p.m. ET, or five minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 10:05 p.m. ET with about 99.9% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

There is no automatic recount provision in Georgia, but a losing candidate may request a recount if the margin is less than or equal to 0.5% of the total vote. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.
news.author: Robert Yoon The Associated Press

They were the top two vote-getters among five contenders in the July 28 all-party special election. Scott received about 46% of the vote, compared to about 38% for Blair.

The winner will serve out the remaining few months of David Scott’s final term. Neither candidate is running in for the next full term in this seat, which begins on Jan. 3, 2027.

Blair was the only candidate in the special election who also ran for the full-term seat. He placed third in the May 19 Democratic primary with about 12% of the vote. State Rep. Jasmine Clark won the primary with 56% of the vote and will face Republican Jonathan Chavez in November. Chavez, who ran unopposed for the GOP nomination, challenged David Scott in the 2024 general election and received about 28% of the vote.

Clark did not file to compete in the special election. Doing so would have required her to resign from her seat in the state Legislature just as Republican Gov. Brian Kemp was calling for a special session to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries in time for the 2028 elections. The state constitution bars state officeholders from seeking a different office with a start date more than 30 days before the end of the officeholder’s current term. The special session did convene, but Republican leaders opted not to take up redistricting.

In recent years, Congressman Scott had faced questions over his age and health. At the time of his death at age 80, he was facing a tough primary challenge from Clark and others as he sought a 13th term.

Georgia’s 13th Congressional District is east and southeast of Atlanta and includes parts of six heavily Democratic counties: Clayton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Henry, Newton and Rockdale. Of the six, the district’s portion of Gwinnett County has the lion’s share of voters, with about 46% of the district electorate in the 2024 general election.

Blair’s best performance in the July 28 special election was in his home base of Gwinnett County, where he received 56% of the vote. Marcye Scott, who lives outside the district in Fulton County as her father did, carried the other five counties in the district, scoring her highest totals in DeKalb, Clayton and Henry.

David Scott won his 2024 reelection bid with about 72% of the vote. In the presidential election that night, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 71% of the vote in the district, compared with about 28% for Republican Donald Trump. Trump had his best performance in the district in Gwinnett County, although that still only amounted to about 35% of the vote.

Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:

When do polls close?

Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the special runoff in the 13th Congressional District.

Who gets to vote?

Any voter registered in the 13th Congressional District may participate in the special runoff.

How many voters are there?

As of Friday, there were about 585,000 registered voters in the 13th Congressional District. Georgia voters do not register by party.

How many people actually vote?

A total of 20,510 votes were cast in the July 28 special election. Turnout in a runoff election tends to be lower than in the election that preceded it.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot? 

About 47% of the total vote in the July 28 special election was cast early in-person or by mail.

As of Friday, about 5,200 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election, with by far the largest share coming from Gwinnett County, followed by Clayton and Rockdale counties.

When are early and absentee votes released?

All six counties in the 13th Congressional District tend to release most or all of their results from early in-person and mail voting in the first vote update of the night, usually before any in-person Election Day results are released.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the July 28 special election, the AP first reported results at 7:05 p.m. ET, or five minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 10:05 p.m. ET with about 99.9% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

There is no automatic recount provision in Georgia, but a losing candidate may request a recount if the margin is less than or equal to 0.5% of the total vote. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.
